issues.item: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: For a natural disaster trauma, this appraisal is a poor thematic fit because it implies an interpersonal perpetrator threat ('who will harm you') rather than danger from impersonal environmental forces. The rest of the profile is built around disaster-related ongoing danger/hypervigilance and intrusive reliving, so this item stands out as clinically incongruent with the specified trauma type.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am
issues.explanation: For a natural disaster trauma, the appraisal 'I acted in ways that go against who I am' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The memory and threat items describe classic fear-based re-experiencing and hypervigilance, but there is no accompanying content suggesting perpetration, moral injury, or a specific action during the disaster that would plausibly drive a strong violated-values appraisal.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life
issues.explanation: 'I have failed in my most important role in life' could occur after a disaster, but here it sits awkwardly with the otherwise generic fear/reliving profile. There are no memory or threat items about failing to protect family, losing dependents, or role-related guilt, so this item lacks support from the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
issues.explanation: 'I need to stay alert' while trying to sleep is more characteristic of an ongoing human threat context than of a completed natural disaster, especially when paired with scanning exits and staying near exits in all buildings. Taken together, these threat items imply anticipation of intentional attack or entrapment rather than the specific threat structure suggested by the trauma type.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life
issues.explanation: 'Failed Role' is not impossible, but it is the least coherent appraisal in this profile for a 65-year-old married male retail worker with natural-disaster trauma. The rest of the profile centers on ongoing danger, hypervigilance, and intrusive reliving; this item instead implies a specific role-based self-evaluation that is not supported by the other selected appraisals, memory, threat, or coping items.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me
issues.explanation: 'Other-Blame Rumination' sits awkwardly with a natural-disaster trauma profile. Blame can occur, but this item specifically focuses on dwelling on what other people have done to me, whereas the rest of the profile describes threat and reliving linked to impersonal environmental danger rather than interpersonal harm or betrayal. Without any corroborating appraisal or memory content involving preventable human actions, this item is clinically hard to reconcile.

vignette:
At 65, Samuel, an African-American retail worker, carries the weight of a devastating natural disaster that struck his town three years ago. When the hurricane hit, Samuel was home with his wife, Martha. They were forced to evacuate as floodwaters rose rapidly, engulfing their neighborhood and leaving destruction in their wake. Samuel vividly remembers the deafening roar of the wind and the sound of debris crashing against their house. That night, as they huddled in a shelter, the terror of uncertainty gripped him; he feared not just for their safety, but also for the future of their lives and home. Since then, Samuel has been unable to shake the memories of that night. They replay in his mind like an endless film loop, each scene as vivid as the last. This reliving of the event feels so real that it often leads him to believe he is still in that moment of chaos, heightening his sense of vulnerability.

In the aftermath of the storm, Samuel found himself increasingly convinced that the world has become a dangerous place. This belief that he was permanently changed fed into his memories of the hurricane, making them feel more vivid and immediate as he replayed the chaos in his mind, emphasizing his sense of vulnerability. This negative appraisal led Samuel to rely on maladaptive strategies, believing that if he stayed alert and prepared, he could somehow protect himself from the dangers he imagined were always lurking just around the corner. This constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof he had that his life had changed beyond repair, shaping his belief that he was permanently altered by the hurricane. This belief that the world is perilous shaped his perception of reality, leading him to see threats in everyday situations and reinforcing the idea that he had to be constantly vigilant. This belief that the world is perilous kept bringing him back to the memories of the hurricane, as if he needed to locate the moment when his sense of safety had shattered. This belief has altered the way he navigates his daily life. He feels that he has permanently changed for the worse, forever marked by fear and anxiety. Every time he enters a room or a building, his instinct is to scan for exits, a habit that feels more like a necessity than a choice. When the threat of danger felt this close, planning his escape routes became a rational response, a way to cope with the overwhelming fear that gripped him. He stays close to exits, ensuring he can escape should another disaster strike. This hyper-vigilance is not just confined to his environment; it seeps into his sleep, making it difficult for him to fall asleep as he feels the need to remain alert, as though danger could emerge from the shadows at any moment. The constant need to monitor his surroundings and plan his escape routes perpetuated his sense of threat, as he never allowed himself to experience any situation long enough to discover it was safe, leaving him in a perpetual state of alarm. The constant sense of threat made him feel as though he had to take protective measures, prompting his maladaptive strategies of scanning the environment and planning escape routes. The result is a cycle of tension and exhaustion that drains both his body and spirit.

Samuel's maladaptive strategies, such as frequent distraction and constant environmental scanning, stem directly from his negative appraisals of the world. He believes that by staying alert and prepared, he can protect himself and his loved ones from harm. However, this vigilance often leads him to perceive threats where there may be none, reinforcing his belief that the world is indeed a perilous place. This constant monitoring of his surroundings became a necessary response to the perceived threat, as he believed that by staying alert, he could prevent something terrible from happening again. Each time he relied on these safety behaviors to navigate his day, Samuel felt a quiet accumulation of evidence that he was more fragile than he wished to admit, confirming his fear that he wasn't getting better. Three years of relying on these strategies had sent him a message he couldn't easily shake: that he must be weaker than others, or he would have been able to overcome this by now. Each time he resorted to his safety behaviors, Samuel felt a quiet accumulation of evidence that confirmed his belief he was unable to cope without them, further solidifying his negative view of himself and the world around him. The reliance on these maladaptive strategies only deepened his negative appraisals, as he became convinced that his inability to navigate life without them meant he was weaker than others, reinforcing the notion that he was permanently damaged. Each time he checks his surroundings or retreats to a corner of a room, he feels a mix of safety and anxiety, as if his actions could somehow shield him from the memories that haunt him. He has come to view this hyper-awareness as a necessary burden; it feels like the only way to prevent the past from repeating itself.

The memories of the hurricane not only haunt his thoughts but also intensify his feelings of threat. The belief that he was permanently changed kept bringing him back to the moment it had happened, as if he needed to locate exactly where he had been lost in that chaos. Each time the vivid recollections of the storm surfaced, Samuel’s thoughts spiraled into the conviction that he must remain vigilant, as if the past was a sign that something terrible was bound to happen again. After each memory replayed, he caught himself thinking that if he couldn't escape those feelings of terror, it must mean there was something fundamentally wrong with him. Samuel tries to cope by distracting himself with television or chores, but even these activities are often interrupted by intrusive thoughts of the disaster. The memories evoke a sense of immediate danger, causing his heart to race and his palms to sweat, as if he is once again facing the storm. Once these memories surfaced, they intensified his sense of threat, creating an overwhelming feeling that he was still trapped in that moment of chaos, unable to escape the danger that seemed ever-present. This sense of threat only deepened his negative appraisal of the world around him, leading him to believe that safety was an illusion he could no longer afford. Each time these memories surfaced, they led him to conclude that he was incapable of protecting himself, deepening his negative appraisal of the world around him. This constant state of alarm, in turn, reinforces his negative view of the world. With each replay of the event in his mind, he becomes more convinced that he must remain on guard, as if the past were a harbinger of future calamities.

As Samuel navigates his life, he is aware of the toll these experiences have taken on his marriage. Martha often expresses concern for his well-being, but Samuel finds it difficult to articulate the depth of his feelings. He fears that sharing his turmoil might burden her further. This sense of isolation compounds his belief that he is permanently damaged, unable to return to the man he once was. He yearns to break free from this cycle but feels trapped in a world that seems fraught with danger.

Recently, Samuel's friends encouraged him to seek help. They noticed his increasing withdrawal and the way he clings to routines shaped by his fears. As he sits in the waiting room, heart racing and palms sweating, he hopes for relief, terrified of what confronting these memories might entail. The thought of healing brings both hope and dread; he longs to reclaim the life he once had, yet fears the pain that may come with revisiting the past. Samuel is at a crossroads, yearning to find a way to dampen the echoes of that night, to discover a renewed sense of safety in a world that now feels anything but secure.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: The vignette does not show how negative appraisals influence memory.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Memory → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not demonstrate how memory influences negative appraisals.
  e.g. "After the image broke through again, she caught herself thinking: if this keeps happening, there must be something deeply wrong with me."
  e.g. "The memory surfaced in the middle of a meeting and she spent the rest of the day convinced that everyone around her could see how broken she was."
  e.g. "Each time the flashback came, the thought that followed it was always the same — that she had let this happen, and that it said something permanent about who she was."
- Threat → Maladaptive Strategies: There is no causal link presented where perceived threat leads to maladaptive strategies.
  e.g. "When the threat felt this close, planning her exit from every room she entered wasn't a symptom — it was just sensible."
  e.g. "She had found that checking the locks twice was the only thing that allowed her body to settle enough to sleep, so she checked them twice."
  e.g. "The only way to move through the world at that level of fear was to make it smaller — fewer places, fewer people, fewer chances for something to go wrong."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals: The vignette lacks a connection where maladaptive strategies lead to negative appraisals.
  e.g. "Three years of avoiding it had told her something she couldn't easily argue with: that she must be more fragile than other people, or she would have been over this by now."
  e.g. "Each time she used a safety behaviour to get through the day, she felt the quiet accumulation of evidence that she couldn't cope without it."
  e.g. "The fact that she still needed to do all of this — the checking, the planning, the long way round — confirmed, in some wordless way, that she wasn't getting better."
